title: Elementary Particles and Conservation Laws
short_intro: Elementary particles are subatomic constituents of matter and radiation that are not known to have any substructure. They are classified fundamentally into fermions and bosons, interacting via four fundamental forces governed by strict conservation laws.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Classification of elementary particles into leptons, mesons, and baryons; basic conservation laws of charge, mass-energy, and linear/angular momentum.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed classification using standard model terminology, strangeness, isospin, baryon number, lepton number, and conservation laws in strong, electromagnetic, and weak interactions.

prerequisites: Conservation laws in mechanics and electrodynamics
Quantum numbers and Pauli's exclusion principle

concept_notes.heading: Classification of Elementary Particles
bullets: Particles are broadly divided based on their spin and interactions into Hadrons (participating in strong interactions) and Leptons (participating in weak and electromagnetic interactions).
Hadrons are further subdivided into Baryons (fermions with half-integral spin, such as protons and neutrons) and Mesons (bosons with integral spin, such as pions).
Leptons include the electron, muon, tau, and their respective neutrinos, all possessing spin-1/2 and obeying Fermi-Dirac statistics.

concept_notes.heading: Conservation Laws in Particle Interactions
bullets: The total electric charge (Q), baryon number (B), and individual lepton numbers (L<sub>e</sub>, L<sub>μ</sub>, L<sub>τ</sub>) are conserved in all known interactions (strong, electromagnetic, and weak).
Strangeness (S) and Isospin (I<sub>3</sub>) are conserved in strong and electromagnetic interactions but can be violated by ΔS = ±1 in weak interactions.
Parity (P), charge conjugation (C), and time reversal (T) are conserved in strong and electromagnetic interactions, while parity and C-parity are maximally violated in weak interactions.

concept_notes.heading: The Quark Model of Hadrons
bullets: Hadrons are not truly elementary; baryons are composed of three quarks (qqq), and mesons are composed of a quark-antiquark pair (qq̄).
The six flavors of quarks are up (u), down (d), strange (s), charm (c), bottom (b), and top (t), each carrying fractional electric charge.
Color charge (red, green, blue) is introduced as the quantum number for the strong interaction, governed by Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD).

concept_notes.heading: Fundamental Interactions and Gauge Bosons
bullets: Gravitational interaction is mediated by the hypothetical graviton; it has negligible effect on subatomic particle scales.
Electromagnetic interaction is mediated by photons, strong interaction by gluons, and weak interaction by W<sup>±</sup> and Z<sup>0</sup> bosons.
Each interaction has a characteristic coupling constant and relative strength, dictating the decay rates and cross-sections of particle reactions.

derivations.title: Threshold Energy for Particle Production
derivations.conditions: A projectile particle of mass m<sub>1</sub> and total energy E incident on a stationary target particle of mass m<sub>2</sub> to produce new particles with total rest mass ∑M.
steps: Write the relativistic energy-momentum four-vector invariant for the initial state in the lab frame: (E + m<sub>2</sub>c<sup>2</sup>)<sup>2</sup> - p<sup>2</sup>c<sup>2</sup> = E<sub>cm</sub><sup>2</sup>.

Express the square of the total center-of-mass energy using E<sup>2</sup> - p<sup>2</sup>c<sup>2</sup> = m<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>c<sup>4</sup>: E<sub>cm</sub><sup>2</sup> = m<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>c<sup>4</sup> + m<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>c<sup>4</sup> + 2Em<sub>2</sub>c<sup>2</sup>.
At threshold, the final products are produced at rest relative to each other in the center-of-mass frame, so the minimum center-of-mass energy is E<sub>cm,min</sub> = (∑M)c<sup>2</sup>.
Equating the invariant mass-energy squares yields the threshold energy condition for the incident particle.

derivations.title: Q-Value of a Nuclear or Particle Reaction
derivations.conditions: Reaction of the form A + B \rightarrow C + D at non-relativistic or relativistic limits.
steps: Write the conservation of total relativistic energy: E_A + E_B = E_C + E_D.
Expand each total energy into its rest mass energy and kinetic energy: (m_A c^2 + K_A) + (m_B c^2 + K_B) = (m_C c^2 + K_C) + (m_D c^2 + K_D).
Define the Q-value as the difference between the total kinetic energy after and before the reaction: Q = (K_C + K_D) - (K_A + K_B).
Substitute back to express Q purely in terms of rest mass energies.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Bubble Chamber Particle Tracks
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Curved tracks of charged particles in a uniform magnetic field showing spirals, vertices, and missing neutral particle paths.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Radius of curvature r = p / (qB) allows determination of momentum, charge sign (from direction of curvature), and lifetime of unstable intermediate states.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Questions identifying particle decay modes and sign of charge from magnetic deflection.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Binding Energy per Nucleon Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of Binding Energy per Nucleon (B.E./A) vs Mass Number (A) rising sharply to a peak around A = 56 and slowly decreasing.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Highlights nuclear stability regions and explains energy release in nuclear fission and fusion.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct conceptual questions on nuclear stability and energetics.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Scattering Cross-Section vs Energy
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A resonance peak curve showing sharp spikes in cross-section at specific energy thresholds.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Indicates the formation of short-lived unstable excited hadron states (resonances) during particle collisions.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting resonance peaks and unstable particle generation.

solved_numericals.question: Determine whether the following reaction is allowed by conservation laws: p + p \rightarrow p + n + \pi^+.
solution_steps: Check Baryon Number (B): Initial B = 1 + 1 = 2. Final B = 1 (proton) + 1 (neutron) + 0 (pion) = 2. Baryon number is conserved.
Check Electric Charge (Q): Initial Q = 1 + 1 = 2. Final Q = 1 (proton) + 0 (neutron) + 1 (pion) = 2. Charge is conserved.
Check Lepton Number (L): Initial L = 0, Final L = 0. Lepton number is conserved.
solved_numericals.answer: Allowed by conservation of charge, baryon number, and lepton number.

solved_numericals.question: Check the validity of the reaction K^- + p \rightarrow \Lambda^0 + \pi^0 using conservation of strangeness, baryon number, and charge.
solution_steps: Write quantum numbers for K^-: B = 0, Q = -1, S = -1. For proton (p): B = 1, Q = 1, S = 0. Initial totals: B = 1, Q = 0, S = -1.
Write quantum numbers for \Lambda^0: B = 1, Q = 0, S = -1. For \pi^0: B = 0, Q = 0, S = 0. Final totals: B = 1, Q = 0, S = -1.
Compare initial and final totals: B_initial = B_final (1 = 1), Q_initial = Q_final (0 = 0), S_initial = S_final (-1 = -1).
solved_numericals.answer: Allowed in strong interactions as strangeness, baryon number, and charge are all conserved.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the threshold kinetic energy of a proton incident on a stationary proton to produce an antiproton via the reaction p + p \rightarrow p + p + p + \bar{p}.
solution_steps: Identify masses: m_1 = m_2 = m_3 = m_4 = m_p = m. Total rest mass of final products ∑M = 4m.
Use the threshold energy formula: E_{th} = \frac{(\sum M)^2 c^2 - m_1^2 c^2 - m_2^2 c^2}{2 m_2}.
Substitute values: E_{th} = \frac{(4m)^2 c^2 - m^2 c^2 - m^2 c^2}{2 m c^2} = \frac{16m^2 c^2 - 2m^2 c^2}{2mc^2} = 7mc^2.
Since total incident energy E = K + mc^2, the threshold kinetic energy is K_{th} = E_{th} - mc^2 = 7mc^2 - mc^2 = 6mc^2.
solved_numericals.answer: 6mc^2 (or 6 times the rest mass energy of a proton, approximately 5.63 GeV)

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes relativistic mechanics apply identically to point-like elementary particles without extended classical boundary corrections.
Quantum field theory framework assumes perturbative convergence, which fails at extremely high energies where strong coupling limits are reached.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Neutrons and protons are elementary particles because they cannot be broken down chemically.
common_misconceptions.correct: Neutrons and protons are composite particles made of three valence quarks.
common_misconceptions.why: High-energy deep inelastic scattering experiments reveal point-like constituents (quarks) inside nucleons.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Strangeness is always conserved in all particle decays.
common_misconceptions.correct: Strangeness is violated in weak interactions (by \Delta S = \pm 1).
common_misconceptions.why: While strong and electromagnetic forces conserve strangeness, the weak force permits quark flavor changing.

quick_revision: Hadrons feel the strong force; leptons do not.
Baryons consist of 3 quarks; mesons consist of a quark-antiquark pair.
Electric charge, baryon number, and lepton numbers are universally conserved.
Strangeness is conserved in strong and electromagnetic interactions but violated in weak interactions.
